newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sales of imported vehicles in Japan rise strongly.
newsitem.headline: Sales of imported vehicles in Japan rise strongly.

text.p: Despite a weak economy, foreign carmakers managed to lure more Japanese motorists into their showrooms last year, pushing up sales of imported cars by 10 percent, the fourth straight year of gains.
The Japan Automobile Importers Association said on Thursday that imported vehicle sales totaled 427,525 units in 1996, surpassing the previous record of 388,162 sold the year before.
Industry analysts said the trend is likely to continue with domestic models looking a bit tired.

"Foreign cars are likely to continue enjoying higher sales this year, in contrast with Japanese cars, as Japanese makers lack attractive models, except for some new recreational vehicles," one analyst said.
The reluctance of the Japanese to buy foreign cars even as they came to dominate the world market was for years a major point of friction with major trading partners.
Excluding the importation of cars built abroad by domestic producers, sales jumped 20 percent.
Analysts said it is now the brand-name appeal of some foreign brands that has attracted buyers.

"Rich people -- and young people in urban areas -- are buying German sedans such as BMW, Audi, Mercedes-Benz and Volkswagen, which have prestige even though they are expensive," said Nikko Research Institute senior analyst Noriyuki Matsushima.
But it wasn't just the luxury cars that proved increasingly attractive.
Customers of Japanese 660cc minicars were also shifting to foreign models such as the Renault Twingo.

Sugiura said sales of imported vehicles may reach 500,000 this year. "Demand for foreign cars is so strong here in Japan. When I visited dealers of Volkswagen and Audi cars recently, they were confident of boosting sales," Sugiura said.
Volkswagen topped the 1996 makers' list for the first time in seven years, with 50,290, up 34.7 percent from a year earlier, helped by strong demand for Golf Wagon and new Polo.
The imports remain a small share of the huge domestic market, however, which is estimated to total some 5.4 million units in 1997.

For December, the news was not so good. The association said sales of imported vehicles fell 2.1 percent in the month from a year earlier to 38,059 vehicles, the first decline in four months on a year-on-year basis.
